content: Progress during the early phase of labor is often slow and accompanied by painful uterine contractions. Women may experience significant distress and a loss of confidence during this stage. Various interventions aimed at providing support and assessment during early labor have been evaluated in prior Cochrane Reviews, and this updated review consolidates and replaces those earlier findings. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of support and assessment interventions during early labor on labor duration, rates of obstetric interventions, and maternal and neonatal outcomes. The review included randomized controlled trials and cluster-randomized trials that evaluated any form of assessment or support intervention during the latent phase of labor. Data were collected and analyzed independently by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. A total of five trials involving 10,421 pregnant women, along with one cluster-randomized trial involving 2,183 women, were included. These trials were conducted in the UK, Canada, and the United States. The interventions studied included early labor assessment versus immediate hospital admission, home visits by midwives versus telephone triage, one-to-one structured midwifery care versus usual care, and hospital assessment using a labor diagnosis algorithm versus standard assessment. The trials were generally at moderate risk of bias, primarily because blinding of participants and staff was not feasible. In one trial involving 209 women, early labor assessment was compared with direct hospital admission. Women in the early assessment group experienced a shorter duration of labor after hospital admission (mean difference: -5.20 hours, 95% CI: -7.06 to -3.34; low-quality evidence). There were no significant differences between groups in rates of cesarean section (RR 0.72, 95% CI: 0.30 to 1.72; very low-quality evidence) or instrumental vaginal birth (RR 0.86, 95% CI: 0.58 to 1.26; very low-quality evidence). Serious maternal morbidity was not reported. Women in the early assessment group were slightly less likely to require epidural analgesia (RR 0.87, 95% CI: 0.78 to 0.98; low-quality evidence) or oxytocin for labor augmentation (RR 0.57, 95% CI: 0.37 to 0.86). They also reported higher satisfaction with their care (mean difference: 16.00, 95% CI: 7.53 to 24.47). No infants were born before hospital admission, and only one infant had a low Apgar score at five minutes (very low-quality evidence). Neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission was not reported. Three studies compared home visits by midwives with telephone triage. One trial reported that home visits had no significant impact on labor duration (mean difference: 0.29 hours, 95% CI: -0.14 to 0.72; 1 trial, 3,474 women; low-quality evidence). There were no significant differences in cesarean section rates (RR 1.05, 95% CI: 0.95 to 1.17; 3 trials, 5,170 women; moderate-quality evidence) or instrumental vaginal birth rates (RR 0.95, 95% CI: 0.79 to 1.15; 2 trials, 4,933 women; low-quality evidence). One trial reported no significant difference in the rate of birth before hospital arrival (RR 1.33, 95% CI: 0.30 to 5.95; 1 trial, 3,474 women). Serious maternal morbidity (RR 0.93, 95% CI: 0.61 to 1.42; 1 trial, 3,474 women; low-quality evidence) and epidural use (RR 0.95, 95% CI: 0.87 to 1.05; 3 trials, 5,168 women; low-quality evidence) were also similar between groups. There were no significant differences in NICU admissions (RR 0.84, 95% CI: 0.50 to 1.42; 3 trials, 5,170 infants; very low-quality evidence) or low Apgar scores at five minutes (RR 1.19, 95% CI: 0.71 to 1.99; 3 trials, 5,170 infants; low-quality evidence). One study involving 5,002 women compared one-to-one structured midwifery care during early labor with usual care. Labor duration was not reported. There were no significant differences in cesarean section rates (RR 0.93, 95% CI: 0.84 to 1.02; high-quality evidence), instrumental vaginal birth rates (RR 0.94, 95% CI: 0.82 to 1.08; high-quality evidence), or serious maternal morbidity (RR 1.13, 95% CI: 0.84 to 1.52; moderate-quality evidence). Epidural use was similar between groups (RR 1.00, 95% CI: 0.99 to 1.01; high-quality evidence). Neonatal outcomes, including NICU admission (RR 0.98, 95% CI: 0.80 to 1.21; high-quality evidence) and low Apgar scores at five minutes (RR 1.07, 95% CI: 0.64 to 1.79; moderate-quality evidence), were also comparable. A cluster-randomized trial involving 2,183 women evaluated the use of a labor diagnosis tool by midwives compared with usual assessment. There were no significant differences in most outcomes, including oxytocin augmentation, epidural use, or rates of instrumental or cesarean births. Women in the intervention group were less likely to be admitted to the hospital at their first presentation. Neonatal outcomes were also similar between groups. In conclusion, assessment and support interventions during early labor do not appear to significantly impact rates of cesarean section, instrumental birth, or birth before hospital arrival. However, some evidence suggests that these interventions may reduce the use of epidural analgesia and increase maternal satisfaction with care. The evidence regarding the use of oxytocin for labor augmentation is mixed. Further research is needed to better understand the effectiveness of early labor assessment compared with immediate hospital admission.
